transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... lately, things have just been feeling a bit off. I work at the plant, you know, on the production line, but they recently asked me to start helping out with the new safety trainings. It’s a nice change of pace, honestly. My supervisor, Gary, he’s a good guy, said I had a knack for explaining things. But since I started doing that, I just... I can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out on the manuals. It's like my skin is just sagging off the bone. 

And then, they took some photos for the company newsletter—they do that every quarter, mostly just highlighting people who hit their five or ten-year marks, but they wanted a shot of the training session. When I saw the picture, I started thinking my face looks completely crooked. Like, lopsided. I mentioned it to my sister, and she said she didn't see it, and a couple of the girls on the line said the same thing, but I don't know. My sister’s always been the pretty one anyway. She used to do pageants when we were kids, if you can believe it. Little Miss Sunshine county winner, 1968. But yeah, the hands and the face... it’s just really bothering me.
Are you worried about anything else besides how your hands and face look?

No, I don't think so. Just my face and my hands. Although, speaking of hands, my sister—the one I was just telling you about—she actually just started making these homemade soaps. Lavender and oatmeal, real fancy stuff. She sells them at the farmer's market down by the old courthouse on weekends. I went down to help her set up her little booth last Sunday, and it was just terribly hot out. Miserable. We had to buy one of those big patio umbrellas just to keep the soap from melting into a puddle on the table. 

The lady next to us was selling these thick knitted sweaters, which made absolutely no sense in that heat, but she said she likes to get a jump on the winter rush. I bought a little blue one for my great-niece, actually, she just turned two. But, um... I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, right, if I was worried about anything else. No, just the hands and the crooked face. That's really it.
Do you think other people can see that your face is crooked?

Well, I mean, they say they can't. Like I told you, my sister and the girls at work said they didn't see anything wrong. But I just feel like they're being polite, you know? People are like that, especially around here. It's like when my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, got that terrible perm last month. It looked like a poodle sat on her head, bless her heart, but did anyone tell her? Of course not. We all just smiled and said it had so much volume. She goes to that salon over on Elm Street, the one next to the bakery. Oh, that bakery has the most wonderful cherry danishes. I used to pick one up every Tuesday on my way to my shift, back when I was on the morning rotation. They use real cherries, not that syrupy stuff out of a can. 

But anyway... what I was saying is, even if they say my face looks fine in those newsletter pictures, I know what I see. It's lopsided. And with my hands looking so old and wrinkly when I'm doing the safety manuals... it's just hard to believe people aren't staring at it all, even if they won't admit it.
Have your thoughts about your face and hands being crooked and wrinkly changed at all since you first noticed them?

Changed? Um... no, not really. It’s pretty much just been exactly the same since I first noticed it. Every time I look down at my hands during those safety trainings, it's just right there, same as always. 

But you know, speaking of the trainings, they just put up a new bulletin board in the breakroom where they pin up all those newsletters and the safety schedules. It’s a cork board, but they painted the frame this absolute awful shade of yellow. Mustard yellow, really. Gary—my supervisor, I mentioned him earlier—he picked the color. He said it was supposed to be cheerful, to boost morale, but it just looks like someone dropped a hot dog on the floor. We had a good laugh about it on Tuesday. 

Tuesday is usually meatloaf day in the cafeteria, which I always skip because the gravy is just too salty, but they actually had chicken salad instead this week. Really good chicken salad, too, with the little green grapes cut up in it and some walnuts. I always mean to make it that way at home, but I never have the patience to sit there and halve all those tiny little grapes. It's so tedious, you know? My sister has one of those little plastic gadgets that slices them all at once, but I just use a paring knife. 

Anyway... I'm sorry, I'm rambling again. Did that answer what you asked? I don't think my thoughts about it have changed, no. It just bothers me the same amount.
Do you ever find yourself trying to stop thinking about your face and hands, but you can't?

Try to stop thinking about them? I don't know that I really try to stop, exactly. It’s not like when you get a song stuck in your head and you just can't shake it no matter what you do. Like yesterday, the girls on the floor always play that oldies station on the radio by the loading dock, and they played that old Monkees song, "Daydream Believer." Well, I had that stuck in my head my entire shift. I was just humming it the whole time I was checking the line. We were running a new batch of the thermal casings, and let me tell you, the company switched plastic suppliers last month to save a few pennies, and the new material smells just awful when it comes out of the molds. Like burnt hair and vinegar. 

I told Gary—my supervisor—that we really need them to turn up the exhaust fans if we're going to keep using this cheap stuff. He said he'd put a work order in, but you know how maintenance is around there. It took them three weeks just to fix the wobbly leg on the breakroom table. I actually ended up folding up a piece of cardboard from a frozen pizza box and sticking it under the leg myself just so our coffees wouldn't spill every time someone sat down. Oh, which reminds me, I need to stop at the grocery store and pick up one of those pizzas for dinner tonight. My sister is coming over to watch our shows, and she loves those thin crust ones with the spinach and the white sauce. Have you ever tried those? They're surprisingly good for being frozen.

But, oh, I'm sorry, I did it again, didn't I? You were asking if I try to stop thinking about my face and my hands. No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really sit there trying to force it out of my head or anything. I just don't like how they look when I notice them, but I'm not fighting with my own brain to stop thinking about it, if that makes sense.
Does thinking about your face and hands affect your ability to do your job or enjoy activities you normally like?

Well, affect my job? No, I wouldn't say it stops me from working or doing my shifts. I still go in, I still do my safety trainings. And I still do my volunteering on the weekends. I help out at the animal shelter, you know, just cleaning cages and walking the smaller dogs. We got this little terrier mix in last week, scruffy little thing named Barnaby. He has one ear that stands straight up and one that flops over, and he just bounces everywhere. The lady who runs the shelter, Susan, she says he’s probably got some Jack Russell in him, which makes sense because he has so much energy. Susan’s been running that place for fifteen years. She actually used to be a dental hygienist before she opened the rescue. Can you imagine? Going from cleaning teeth to cleaning up after dogs all day. But she loves it. She has this big van she uses to transport them to the adoption events at the PetSmart over on Highway 9. That highway is getting so congested lately, though. They’ve been doing road work on the overpass since last spring and it's just a mess. I try to take the back roads when I can, past the old drive-in theater. It's a shame they closed that place down, I used to love going there when I was younger.

But, um, what was I saying? Oh, right, my job and things. So no, it hasn't stopped me from doing what I need to do. I will admit, though, I am a lot slower getting ready in the mornings, especially on the days I have to stand up in front of everyone for those trainings. I just... I spend more time trying to fix my hair so maybe it distracts from my face, or making sure my sleeves are pulled down over my hands. And I've definitely started ducking out of the way when they bring out the camera for the company newsletter. I just don't want to be in the pictures anymore. And I guess... well, I do hesitate a bit more before going to the shelter potlucks or the girls' nights out. I still go, usually, but I just don't enjoy them as easily as I used to because I'm worrying about how I look. But I still go! Just, you know, maybe I stand a little closer to the back of the room.
Do you think it's possible that your face and hands might look normal to other people, even if they look crooked and wrinkly to you?

Normal to other people? Oh, I suppose it's possible. I mean, Gary hasn't said anything about it, and he notices everything. Like last week, he noticed I was using the blue pens instead of the black ones on the inventory sheets. The company policy says we're supposed to use black ink for all official documentation, which I think is a bit silly, really. Blue ink is just as easy to read, don't you think? And honestly, the blue pens we get from the supply closet just write so much smoother. The black ones always skip, and then you have to scribble on a piece of scrap paper to get the ink flowing again. 

I keep a little notepad right by my station just for that. It's one of those promotional notepads from a local realtor. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, gave it to me. She just sold her house last month. Moved down to Florida to be closer to her daughter. She had this beautiful garden in her backyard—rose bushes all along the fence, and these huge hydrangeas. I always told her she should enter them in the county fair, but she said it was too much fuss. Now the new owners have moved in, and I swear, they haven't watered those hydrangeas once. It just breaks my heart to see them wilting. I was half tempted to sneak over there with my watering can the other evening, but I didn't want them to think I was some crazy old lady snooping around their yard in the dark. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my hands and face looking normal to other people. Yeah, I guess maybe they could look fine to someone else. I don't know for sure, because no one's ever brought it up, but it's possible they just don't see what I see.
Do you think your face could ever look not crooked to you, or is that something you're certain about?

Could my face ever look not crooked to me? I don't know, I'm not really sure if I'm certain about it. I don't know if you can ever be completely certain about anything, really. You think things are going to stay one way and then they just change out of nowhere. Like the bus schedule. They completely changed the routes for the 42 line last week and didn't put up a single sign at the shelter. I was standing out there for forty-five minutes on Tuesday morning. It was freezing, too! We had that frost advisory, and the wind was just whipping right through my coat. 

My sister, the one I mentioned who came over for the pizza, she keeps telling me to buy one of those heavy down coats from Macy's. But they are just so expensive now. I saw one in their Sunday circular that was almost two hundred dollars. Who pays two hundred dollars for a coat just to stand at the bus stop? I usually just wear my old wool one, the navy blue one I got at the outlet mall years ago. The zipper gets a little stuck sometimes, right near the bottom, but if you rub a little piece of bar soap on the zipper teeth, it slides right up. My grandmother taught me that trick. She used to sew all her own clothes. She had this big heavy Singer sewing machine, the kind built right into the wooden table with the cast-iron pedal on the bottom. I used to love watching the needle go up and down so fast. 

But, oh dear, I'm rambling again. I'm sorry. What were you asking me? Oh, right, if I'm certain it'll always look crooked to me. I really couldn't tell you. I guess I'm not completely certain, I just don't know. Right now, that's just what I see when I look in the mirror, but I suppose I don't know for sure what the future holds.
Do you think there's any possibility that your perception of your face and hands might be different from reality?

Different from reality? Well, I suppose... I don't really know. Reality is such a funny word, isn't it? It always makes me think of those reality television shows. My niece, Sarah, she got me hooked on that British baking one. Have you ever watched it? They make the most incredible things out of just flour and water. I tried baking my own bread a couple of years ago, you know, when everyone was doing the sourdough thing. But mine just smelled terrible, like old gym socks, and it never rose right. I'm pretty sure my oven runs cold. It's this old Kenmore I've had since the late nineties. The dial says 350, but I bet it's barely hitting 325. I had a repairman out last month, and he told me they don't even manufacture the parts for it anymore. Nice young man, though. He even helped me change the lightbulb over the kitchen sink while he was here. Those recessed lights are just impossible to reach, even with my step stool. I bought one of those folding ones at Target, but you have to be so careful because it pinches your fingers right at the hinge if you don't grab it just right. 

But, oh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry. You were asking about reality, and my face and hands. Honestly, I just don't know. I really couldn't tell you if my perception is different from what's actually there. Maybe it is? I just... I'm not sure. It's hard to know what's real when you're the one looking through your own eyes, you know?
Has your concern about your face and hands affected your relationships with friends or family?

Affected my relationships? Well, I still see people. I mean, it hasn't stopped me from working or doing my volunteer shifts at the library. I've been helping sort the donated books on Thursday afternoons for years now. You wouldn't believe what people donate, honestly. Last week, I found a whole box of encyclopedias from 1982! I told the head librarian, Brenda, I said, Brenda, nobody is going to use these, Pluto is still listed as a regular planet in here! But she insists we put them on the sale cart for fifty cents apiece. Brenda is a bit of a hoarder, if you ask me. Her desk is just covered in old coffee mugs and sticky notes. I don't know how she gets any work done. I have to keep my station at the plant completely spotless or I just can't focus on the production line. My supervisor is a real stickler for a clean workspace, too. He used to be in the Navy, so everything has to be shipshape. He even polishes his boots every single morning. 

Oh, listen to me going on about Brenda and the boots. I'm sorry, I get so easily sidetracked. You were asking about my family and friends, and if this is affecting things. 

Well, like I said, I haven't stopped working or volunteering, but... I have noticed I'm a lot slower getting ready for things. Even just getting ready for the regular safety trainings at work takes me longer now because I'm fussing with how I look. And I definitely find myself hesitating before social events that I used to enjoy so easily. Like my niece's birthday dinner last weekend... I almost didn't go. And when they brought the cake out and everyone was taking pictures, I started ducking out of the photos. I just made an excuse to go check on the coffee in the kitchen so I wouldn't have to be in them.
Do you think someone else, looking at you, would see your face as crooked?

Would someone else see it? Well, I suppose that's the whole reason I'm here, really. I came in because since I started helping with the safety trainings at the plant, I just can't seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I'm pointing things out on the diagrams. We use these big laminated charts, you know, the ones that show all the emergency shut-off valves. And the lamination is so glossy, it catches the fluorescent lights right above the training room. They just put in those new LED bulbs, too, the bright white ones that make everything look like a hospital. My eyes get so tired by the end of the shift. I've been meaning to get my prescription checked at the eye doctor. Dr. Aris, over on Main Street. He's got such a nice waiting room, always has those big glossy magazines, the ones about home decorating. I love looking at the kitchens. Who has a kitchen with two islands? Honestly, you'd need roller skates just to make a cup of tea! 

Oh, goodness, I'm wandering off again, aren't I? I'm sorry. You were asking if other people see my face as crooked. Well, I start thinking my face looks crooked in the company newsletter photos—they take a picture of the safety team every quarter—but when I bring it up, other people say they don't see it. They tell me I look fine, but I just... I don't know how they can't see it when it's right there.
Do you think your concerns about your face and hands might be exaggerated or not entirely based on how you actually look?

Exaggerated? I... I don't know. It's hard to say if I'm blowing it out of proportion. I mean, my sister always used to tell me I made mountains out of molehills. She's the dramatic one, though, if you ask me. She called me last Tuesday in an absolute panic because she couldn't find her favorite gardening gloves. The green ones with the little rubber dots on the palms. She loves those gloves. She grows the most beautiful tomatoes, though. Beefsteaks, big as your head! She cans them every August. My kitchen gets so hot when we do the canning, the steam just fogs up the windows. I have those nice double-pane windows, but they still get condensation. The salesman said they were energy efficient, but my heating bill last winter was still through the roof. I tried calling the gas company about it, but you just sit on hold listening to that awful elevator music for forty-five minutes before a real person picks up. 

Oh, dear, I'm doing it again. I'm sorry, my mind just goes a mile a minute sometimes. You asked if my concerns were exaggerated. I really couldn't tell you. I know what I see when I look in the mirror or look down at my hands during the safety meetings, but... I don't know if it's exaggerated. I just know it bothers me.
Do you think it's possible that your face and hands look normal, but you just can't see it that way?

Normal? I... I mean, I suppose it's possible. It's just so hard to wrap my head around that when I see what I see. It's like when you look at a magic eye poster, you know? My grandson, Leo, he loves those things. He got a whole book of them for his birthday. He's nine now, growing like a weed. He needs new shoes every three months, I swear. My daughter takes him to that discount shoe place out on Route 9, but I keep telling her, you get what you pay for with shoes. If you don't have good arch support, your back is going to pay for it later. I learned that the hard way standing on the concrete floor at the plant all day. I finally had to buy those expensive orthopedic inserts. They cost an arm and a leg, but my sciatica hasn't flared up since I got them. 

Oh, listen to me, going on about shoes and backs. I'm sorry. You were asking if maybe I just can't see that I look normal. I don't know. Maybe? I really couldn't say for sure. I just know what I see in the mirror.

Do you think it's possible that your face and hands look exactly the same as they did before you started noticing these issues, and that your concern about them is not based on any actual change in your appearance?

Exactly the same as before? Well, I suppose I haven't really kept track. I was actually looking at some old photos just this past weekend, trying to see if I could tell. They were in those old magnetic albums, you know the ones with the sticky pages and the clear plastic sheet you peel back? They say those are just terrible for preserving pictures because the glue turns yellow and ruins the backing. My mother bought a whole stack of them from the Sears catalog back in the eighties. Gosh, do you remember the Sears catalog? We used to get the big Christmas Wish Book every year. My brother and I would circle the things we wanted with a red marker. He always wanted those Hess toy trucks. He had a whole collection of them on a shelf in his bedroom, but his wife made him box them all up when they moved down to Florida. They live near Tampa now. The humidity down there is just unbearable, my hair frizzes up into a giant puff the second I step out of the airport... 

Oh, goodness, I'm so sorry. I completely lost my train of thought again. Florida, honestly. You were asking if nothing actually changed about my appearance, if it's all exactly the same as before. I... I really couldn't tell you. I'm not sure. I can't say for certain if they look the exact same as they used to. I just know that when I look at my face and my hands now, it's all I can focus on.
Do you think it's possible that your concerns about your face and hands are not based on anything that's actually there?

Not based on anything that's actually there? Like I'm just imagining it? I... I don't know how that could be, but I guess anything is possible. It's funny you mention imagining things, though. We had this safety inspector come into the plant last month, and he swore he saw a spark near the main conveyor belt. We had to shut down production for three whole hours while the maintenance guys crawled all over the machinery. Three hours! Do you know how many units we lost? My supervisor, Jerry, he was just livid. His face gets this awful shade of purple when he's mad, right up to the tips of his ears. He takes blood pressure medication, but he still eats those salty pretzels from the vending machine every afternoon. I keep telling him, Jerry, you're going to give yourself a heart attack with all that sodium. But you can't tell him anything. He's stubborn as a mule. His wife makes these wonderful low-sodium lunches for him, chicken and rice and broccoli, and he just leaves them in the breakroom fridge until they go bad. It's a shame, really, wasting good food like that with the price of groceries these days. A dozen eggs is almost five dollars at the Stop & Shop...

Oh, dear me. I'm rambling again, aren't I? I am so sorry. You asked if my concerns weren't based on anything real. I just... I really couldn't say. I don't know if I'm imagining it or not. I just know it feels very real to me when I look at myself.
Do you think it's possible that your face and hands look perfectly normal, but you're just unable to see them that way?

Perfectly normal? I... well, I guess anything is possible. It’s hard to say what perfectly normal even means, though. It’s kind of like when I went to get my eyes checked last fall. Dr. Evans, he’s been my optometrist for twenty years, and he told me I finally needed bifocals. When I put them on for the first time, the whole floor looked like it was tilted sideways. I swear I almost tumbled right down the front steps of his clinic. They have those terribly steep concrete steps, you know, with the black metal railing that gets just blisteringly hot in the summer? I burned my palm on a railing just like that at the municipal pool back when my daughter was little. We were trying to get her to take swimming lessons, but she absolutely hated the water. She would cling to my neck like a little monkey, just screaming bloody murder. We finally had to pull her out of the class and get a partial refund. They fought me on the refund, too, the parks department can be so stingy with their policies...

Oh, good heavens, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry, I just start talking and my brain goes right off the rails. You were asking if they look normal and I just can't see it. I... I honestly don't have a good answer for you. I just don't know. I really couldn't say if that's what's happening or not.
Do you think it's possible that your concerns about your appearance are not based in reality?

Not based in reality? Well... I suppose it's hard to know what reality even is sometimes. It makes me think of all those reality television shows my sister watches. She's just obsessed with that one where they bake the cakes that look like everyday objects. She called me last Tuesday—or maybe it was Wednesday, because it was raining and I had to put the patio cushions in the shed—anyway, she was going on and on about a cake that looked exactly like a pair of muddy work boots. Which reminds me, I really need to get new inserts for my shoes for the line at the plant. Standing on that concrete floor for eight hours a day just completely ruins your arches. I used to buy those Dr. Scholl's inserts, but I swear they changed the foam they use. Everything is just made cheaper these days. It's just like the toaster I bought at Target last month. Two weeks in, and the lever wouldn't even stay down. I had to stand there physically holding it just to get a single piece of rye bread toasted for my breakfast...

Oh, for heaven's sake. Listen to me going on about toast. I am so sorry, my mind just wanders right off. You were asking if my concerns aren't based in reality. I... I really don't know. I can't tell you for sure one way or the other. It feels very real to me, but I just don't have a good answer for you.
Do you think it's possible that your face and hands look exactly as they have always looked, and that your concern about their appearance is entirely in your mind?

Entirely in my mind? Well... I suppose anything is possible, isn't it? The mind is a funny thing. It reminds me of my Aunt Clara, she used to swear she could hear the radio playing even when it was unplugged. We finally figured out it was just the wind whistling through the old storm windows at her house on Elm Street. Those windows were original to the house, you know, built back in 1922. They had that beautiful wavy glass that you just can't find anymore. I tried to get some for a craft project I was doing last winter—I was making these little terrariums out of old picture frames—but the antique store downtown wanted an absolute fortune for just one pane. It's ridiculous how much they charge for things that used to just be considered junk. Like those old mason jars, people pay twenty dollars for a blue one now! I must have thrown out dozens of those when we cleared out my mother's basement. She used to can her own tomatoes every August. The whole house would smell like basil and vinegar for a week... 

Oh, goodness gracious. There I go again, talking your ear off about tomatoes and old glass. I am so sorry, I just get sidetracked so easily. You were asking if it's all in my mind, if I look the same as I always have. I just... I really couldn't say for sure. I don't know if it's all in my head or not. I just don't have a solid answer for you on that.
Do you think your concerns about your face and hands are based on something that isn't real?

Based on something that isn't real? I... well, it's so hard to know what's real and what isn't these days, isn't it? It makes me think of those artificial plants they sell at Michael's now. I was in there just last week looking for some yarn—I'm trying to knit a blanket for my neighbor's new grandbaby, a little boy, they named him Oliver—and I walked right past this display of ferns. I swear to you, I reached out and touched one because I couldn't believe it wasn't a real plant. The texture of the leaves, the little brown spots they painted on them... it's amazing what they can manufacture. My husband used to work at a plastics factory back in the eighties, before they moved all the jobs overseas. He would come home smelling like melted chemicals, it was just awful. We had to wash his work clothes separate from everything else, and even then, I felt like the smell lingered in the washing machine. We had this old Kenmore washer, the kind that was avocado green, you remember those? It lasted us twenty-five years before the motor finally gave out. They just don't build appliances to last like that anymore...

Oh, my stars. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so, so sorry. My mouth just runs away from me. You were asking if my worries about my face and hands are based on something that isn't real. I... I just don't know. I really couldn't tell you. It feels real to me, but I just don't have a good answer for whether it actually is or not.
Do you think your face and hands look the way you think they do to anyone else?

Do other people see it? Well... they tell me they don't. That's actually the main reason I came in to see you. Recently they had me start helping out with the safety trainings at the plant, and when I'm up there pointing things out on the diagrams or the machines, I just can't seem to stop noticing how horribly wrinkly and uneven my hands look. And then they put my picture in the company newsletter, and my face looks completely crooked to me. But when I mention it, the other girls say they don't see it at all. 

Which is funny, because they usually notice every little thing. Like my friend Brenda, she noticed right away that they switched the type of paper they print that newsletter on. It used to be a nice, thick matte finish, but now it's this cheap glossy stuff that leaves fingerprint smudges everywhere if you even just hold it. It reminds me of the Sunday newspaper back in the nineties. My husband would sit in his recliner reading the sports section, and his fingers would just be coated in black ink. I had to buy that heavy-duty orange pumice soap just to get his hands clean before church. You know, the kind mechanics use? It smelled so strongly of artificial oranges, it would make my nose itch just walking past the bathroom sink. We used to keep it in this little ceramic dish that my daughter made in her middle school art class. It was supposed to be a turtle, I think, but the glaze melted funny in the kiln...

Oh, for Pete's sake. Look at me, talking about orange soap and ceramic turtles. I am so sorry, my brain just takes a left turn and keeps driving. You asked if anyone else sees what I see. Like I said, they tell me they don't see the crookedness or the wrinkles at all, even though it's absolutely all I can look at.

doctor.intent: identify chief complaint
doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I came in because since I started helping with the safety trainings, I can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out, and then I start thinking my face looks crooked in the newsletter photos even though other people say they don’t see it.

patient.answer:
Well, I came in because... lately, things have just been feeling a bit off. I work at the plant, you know, on the production line, but they recently asked me to start helping out with the new safety trainings. It’s a nice change of pace, honestly. My supervisor, Gary, he’s a good guy, said I had a knack for explaining things. But since I started doing that, I just... I can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out on the manuals. It's like my skin is just sagging off the bone. 

And then, they took some photos for the company newsletter—they do that every quarter, mostly just highlighting people who hit their five or ten-year marks, but they wanted a shot of the training session. When I saw the picture, I started thinking my face looks completely crooked. Like, lopsided. The symptom profile does not contain an item specifically for 'Insight' or 'Delusional Beliefs', as S067 covers the preoccupation itself, S068 covers repetitive behaviors, and functional_impairment covers the impact. Therefore, 'None' is the most appropriate response.

patient.answer:
Entirely in my mind? Well... I suppose anything is possible, isn't it? The mind is a funny thing. It reminds me of my Aunt Clara, she used to swear she could hear the radio playing even when it was unplugged. We finally figured out it was just the wind whistling through the old storm windows at her house on Elm Street. Those windows were original to the house, you know, built back in 1922. They had that beautiful wavy glass that you just can't find anymore. I tried to get some for a craft project I was doing last winter—I was making these little terrariums out of old picture frames—but the antique store downtown wanted an absolute fortune for just one pane. It's ridiculous how much they charge for things that used to just be considered junk. Like those old mason jars, people pay twenty dollars for a blue one now! I must have thrown out dozens of those when we cleared out my mother's basement. She used to can her own tomatoes every August. The whole house would smell like basil and vinegar for a week... 

Oh, goodness gracious. There I go again, talking your ear off about tomatoes and old glass. I am so sorry, I just get sidetracked so easily. You were asking if it's all in my mind, if I look the same as I always have. I just... I really couldn't say for sure. I don't know if it's all in my head or not. I just don't have a solid answer for you on that.

doctor.question: Do you think your concerns about your face and hands are based on something that isn't real?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking about insight/delusional beliefs regarding the perceived defects (whether the concerns are not real/all in the mind). The patient's symptom profile covers Preoccupation with Appearance (S067), Repetitive Behaviors (S068), and Functional Impairment, but does not include a specific symptom for insight or delusional beliefs (e.g., absent insight/delusional beliefs). Therefore, none of the provided symptom profile items directly match this question.

patient.answer:
Based on something that isn't real? I... well, it's so hard to know what's real and what isn't these days, isn't it? It makes me think of those artificial plants they sell at Michael's now. I was in there just last week looking for some yarn—I'm trying to knit a blanket for my neighbor's new grandbaby, a little boy, they named him Oliver—and I walked right past this display of ferns. I swear to you, I reached out and touched one because I couldn't believe it wasn't a real plant. The texture of the leaves, the little brown spots they painted on them... it's amazing what they can manufacture. My husband used to work at a plastics factory back in the eighties, before they moved all the jobs overseas. He would come home smelling like melted chemicals, it was just awful. We had to wash his work clothes separate from everything else, and even then, I felt like the smell lingered in the washing machine. We had this old Kenmore washer, the kind that was avocado green, you remember those? It lasted us twenty-five years before the motor finally gave out. They just don't build appliances to last like that anymore...

Oh, my stars. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so, so sorry. My mouth just runs away from me. You were asking if my worries about my face and hands are based on something that isn't real. I... I just don't know. I really couldn't tell you. It feels real to me, but I just don't have a good answer for whether it actually is or not.

doctor.question: Do you think your face and hands look the way you think they do to anyone else?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I came in because since I started helping with the safety trainings, I can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m pointing things out, and then I start thinking my face looks crooked in the newsletter photos even though other people say they don’t see it.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if the patient thinks their face and hands look the way they perceive them to anyone else, which relates to the 'not observable or appear slight to others' aspect of the Preoccupation with Appearance symptom.

patient.answer:
Do other people see it? Well... they tell me they don't. That's actually the main reason I came in to see you. Recently they had me start helping out with the safety trainings at the plant, and when I'm up there pointing things out on the diagrams or the machines, I just can't seem to stop noticing how horribly wrinkly and uneven my hands look. And then they put my picture in the company newsletter, and my face looks completely crooked to me. But when I mention it, the other girls say they don't see it at all. 

Which is funny, because they usually notice every little thing. Like my friend Brenda, she noticed right away that they switched the type of paper they print that newsletter on. It used to be a nice, thick matte finish, but now it's this cheap glossy stuff that leaves fingerprint smudges everywhere if you even just hold it. It reminds me of the Sunday newspaper back in the nineties. My husband would sit in his recliner reading the sports section, and his fingers would just be coated in black ink. I had to buy that heavy-duty orange pumice soap just to get his hands clean before church. You know, the kind mechanics use? It smelled so strongly of artificial oranges, it would make my nose itch just walking past the bathroom sink. We used to keep it in this little ceramic dish that my daughter made in her middle school art class. It was supposed to be a turtle, I think, but the glaze melted funny in the kiln...

Oh, for Pete's sake. Look at me, talking about orange soap and ceramic turtles. I am so sorry, my brain just takes a left turn and keeps driving. You asked if anyone else sees what I see. Like I said, they tell me they don't see the crookedness or the wrinkles at all, even though it's absolutely all I can look at.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's excessive preoccupation with a perceived defect in their appearance, specifically their face and hands, which is not noticeable to others, suggests a diagnosis of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD). The patient's symptoms, such as repeatedly checking their appearance, trying to hide or camouflage the perceived flaws, and avoiding social situations due to feelings of self-consciousness, are consistent with BDD.
